name: Salafi movement
scope: The contemporary Sunni Salafi movement as the scholarship defines it: a purist creed and method that seeks to return to the religion of the salaf (the first three generations of Muslims), relying on Quran and Sunnah, opposing innovation (bid'a) and, in most strands, blind adherence to a legal school (taqlid), with Ibn Taymiyya as a main medieval reference (Wiktorowicz, Lauzière, Qadhi). It covers the purist (quietist) and political strands that Wiktorowicz distinguishes and the positions Qadhi lists among Salafi groups. It excludes the jihadi strand (the separate Salafi jihadism ideology), Wahhabism and Ahl-i Hadith as their own movements, and the 19th-century modernist reformers (Afghani, Abduh), whom Lauzière shows were not called Salafis in their own time and whom modern Salafis reject as rationalists. Positions are taken from the sources' accounts of Salafi tenets and from the writings of its key figures, not from critics.

summary: Salafism is a Sunni revival movement that seeks to return to the creed and practice of the first three generations of Muslims, holding that God alone legislates and that there is one correct reading of the Qur'an and Sunna. Its purist strand focuses on propagation and avoids politics; its politicos enter parties and protest but stop short of revolution. Most Salafis, unlike the jihadis, reject targeting noncombatants and rebellion against rulers.

notes: Themes searched: ruler obedience and rebellion, democracy and elections, secularism, scripture and reason, hijab, apostasy, homosexuality, blasphemy, interest, gender roles, violence against civilians. Only church-state, scripture, reason, interpretation, public role of religion, rebellion and civilians are stated in the defining sources; Salafis disagree among themselves on democracy and parties, so those stay null. Fatwa sites (islamqa) could not be tied to a key figure or key work, so no answers rest on them.
